parole.significato: Forms plurals from words of Arabic origin.
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish ـات, from Arabic ـَات (-āt).

parole.significato: Forms adverbs from words of Arabic origin.
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish ـاً (-en), from Arabic ـًا (-an).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish ـی (-î), from Arabic ـِيّ (-iyy).

parole.significato: Used to make municipality, corporation, discipline names.
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish ـیه (-iye), from Arabic ـِيَّة (-iyya). Doublet of -iyet.

parole.significato: Used to make noun meaning state of an adjective
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish ـِیَّت (-iyyet), from Arabic ـِيَّة (-iyya). Doublet of -iye.

parole.significato: felt (a non-woven cloth that is produced by matting, condensing and pressing woollen fibres)
parole.testo: From Arabic عَبَاءَة (ʕabāʔa).
From Ottoman Turkish آبا (aba), from Arabic آباء (ʔābāʔ).

parole.significato: A religious devotee in radical Sufism who has attained a high level of spirituality, comparable to a sannyasi in Hindui…
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish ابدال (abdal, “a kind of heedless, disinterested, good-natured man, who takes no care for the morrow”), from Arabic أَبْدَال (ʔabdāl, “compensations, beggar, careless man”). Doublet of aptal (“dumb, stupid”).
From Ottoman Turkish عبث, from Arabic عَبَث (ʕabaṯ).

Inherited from Ottoman Turkish آبده (ābide), from Arabic آبِدة (ʔābida), from آبِد (ʔābid), active participle of أَبَدَ (ʔabada). The sense of monument first attested around 1908 with respect to the Monument of Liberty (Âbide-i Hürriyet) then under construction in Istanbul.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish آبراش (abraş), from Arabic أَبْرَش (ʔabraš, “dappled, mottled”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عبوس الوجه (’abusü l-vech), from Arabic عَبُوسُ ٱلْوَجْه (ʕabūsu l-wajh).

parole.significato: Used to add a meaning of curiosity, indecision or doubt, and sometimes courtesy. Roughly equivalent to “I wonder (if/wh…
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish عجبا (ʿacaba), from Arabic عَجَبًا (ʕajaban), adverbial accusative of عَجَب (ʕajab, “astonishment, wonder, amazement”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عجایب (acayip), from Arabic عَجَائِب (ʕajāʔib, “wonders, marvels”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عجله (ʼacele, “rush, haste”), from Arabic عَجَلَة (ʕajala).

parole.significato: In an urgent manner; urgently, promptly, without delay.
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عجلةً (ʿaceleten), from Arabic عَجَلَةً (ʕajalatan) adverbial accusative of عَجَلَة (ʕajala), from عَجِلَ (ʕajila, “to hurry”).

parole.significato: a compound maqam in Turkish classical music
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عجم (ʿacem), from Arabic عَجَم (ʕajam).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عجمی (acemi, “janissary recruit”), from Arabic عَجَمِيّ (ʕajamiyy, “non-Arab, foreigner”).
From Ottoman Turkish عاجل (“hasty; transitory; prompt”), from Arabic عَاجِل (ʕājil, “urgent”), from عَجِلَ (ʕajila, “to be urgent; to hurry”).

parole.significato: In an urgent manner; urgently, promptly, without delay.
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عاجلاً (ʿācilen), from Arabic عَاجِلًا (ʕājilan), adverbial accusative of عَاْجِل (ʕājil), from عَجِلَ (ʕajila, “to hurry”). By surface analysis, acil + -en.
From Arabic عَجِين (ʕajīn).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عجز (acz), from Arabic عَجْز (ʕajz).

parole.significato: Cucumis melo var. flexuosus, a slender, long, ligh green fruit from the melon family; Armenian cucumber, snake cucumber…
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish آجور (acur, “a kind of cucumber”), shares common origin with Arabic عَجُّور (ʕajjūr), derived from Byzantine Greek ἀγγούριν (angoúrin), derived from Ancient Greek άγγος (ángos).
From Ottoman Turkish عضله (adale), from Arabic عَضَلَة (ʕaḍala, “muscle”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish آدم (adam), from Old Anatolian Turkish آدم (âdem), borrowed from Arabic آدَم (ʔādam), borrowed from Biblical Hebrew אָדָם (āḏā́m). Doublet of Adem.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عددی (ʿadedi), from Arabic عَدَدِيّ (ʕadadiyy), from عَدَد (ʕadad, “number”) + ـِيّ (-iyy, nisba suffix).
From Ottoman Turkish عدم, from Arabic عَدَم (ʕadam).
From Ottoman Turkish عدسه (adese), from Arabic عَدَسَة (ʕadasa).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عدد (aded, “amount”), from Arabic عَدَد (ʕadad, “number”)
From Ottoman Turkish عادی (adi), from Arabic عَادِيّ (ʕādiyy, “normal”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عادل, from Arabic عَادِل (ʕādil).

parole.significato: court of law (court presided over by a judge)
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish عدلیه (adliye), from Arabic عَدْلِيَّة (ʕadliyya).
From Ottoman Turkish عفو ('afv), from Arabic عَفْو (ʕafw).
From Ottoman Turkish آفاق, from Arabic آفَاق (ʔāfāq), plural of أُفُق (ʔufuq).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish خفقان (hafakan), from Arabic خَفَقَان (ḵafaqān).
From Ottoman Turkish آفاقی (afaki), from Arabic آفَاقِيّ (ʔāfāqiyy).

parole.significato: To lose control on oneself because of being astonished, bewildered, boggled
parole.testo: From afal afal, aval aval + -la (verbalizing suffix), from Arabic أحول (ʔaḥwal, “cross-eyed”). Originally a dialectical term brought into the written standard during the language reform. See also Ottoman Turkish آفال طاپال (afal tapal, “dumbfounded, dumbstruck”).
From Arabic عَفَن (ʕafan).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish آفت (afet), from Arabic آفَة (ʔāfa).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عافیت (âfiyet), from Arabic عَافِيَة (ʕāfiya).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish آفیون (afyon), from Arabic أَفْيُون (ʔafyūn), from Ancient Greek ὄπιον (ópion). Cognate with English opium.
Borrowed from Arabic عِقَال (ʕiqāl). Doublet of ıkal (“shackles”).
From Ottoman Turkish اهالی (ehali, ahali), from Arabic أَهَالِي (ʔahālī).
From Ottoman Turkish احباب (ahbab, ahbap), from Arabic أَحْبَاب (ʔaḥbāb), plural of حَبِيب (ḥabīb).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عهدی, from Arabic عَهْدِيّ (ʕahdiyy). By surface analysis, ahit (“oath; agreement”) + -i (nisba suffix).
From Ottoman Turkish آخر (âhir), from Arabic آخِر (ʔāḵir).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish آخرت (âhiret), from Arabic اَلْآخِرَة (al-ʔāḵira, “the hereafter”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عهد, ultimately from Arabic عَهْد (ʕahd).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish آخذه (ahize), from Arabic آخِذَة f (ʔāḵiḏa, literally “the taking one, which receives”). The sense is a calque from French récepteur.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish اخلاق (aḫlaḳ), from Arabic أَخْلَاق (ʔaḵlāq).
From Ottoman Turkish اخلاقی (ahlâkî), from Arabic أَخْلَاقِيّ (ʔaḵlāqiyy). By surface analysis, ahlak (“morality”) + -i (nisba suffix).

parole.significato: four bodily fluids, referred to as the cardinal humours
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish اخلاط (ahlât), from Arabic أَخْلَاْط (ʔaḵlāṭ), plural of Arabic خِلْط (ḵilṭ); which is also borrowed into Ottoman Turkish as خلط (hılt, halt).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish احمق, from Arabic أَحْمَق (ʔaḥmaq).
From Ottoman Turkish احمر, from Arabic أَحْمَر (ʔaḥmar).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish اخرس (ahras), from Arabic أَخْرَس (ʔaḵras).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish اخشاب (ahşap), from earlier اخشب, borrowed from Arabic أَخْشَب (ʔaḵšab).

parole.significato: due, membership fee, money paid members of associations, organizations, or clubs at regular intervals
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عاﺋﺪﺍﺕ (ʼaydat), plural of عاﺋﺪه (ʼayde, “income, revenue, profit”), from Arabic عَائِدَة (ʕāʔida, “return, gain, yield”).
From Ottoman Turkish عائله ('aile), from Arabic عائِلَة (ʕāʔila).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عائد, عاید (aid, ait), from Arabic عَائِد (ʕāʔid). Compare Azerbaijani aid.
From Ottoman Turkish عقار, from Arabic عَقَار (ʕaqār).

parole.significato: a piece of landed property that yields a revenue
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish عقارت (akaret), from Arabic عَقَار (ʕaqār).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عقیده (akide), from Arabic عَقِيدَة (ʕaqīda)
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عقیق, borrowed form Arabic عَقِيق (ʕaqīq), borrowed from Aramaic עקיק.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عاقل ('âkil), from Arabic عَاقِل (ʕāqil).
From Ottoman Turkish عكس (aks, akis), from Arabic عَكْس (ʕaks, “opposite”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عقد (ʿakid), from Arabic عَقْد (ʕaqd)
From Ottoman Turkish عقلی (aklî), from Arabic عَقْلِيّ (ʕaqliyy). By surface analysis, akıl (“mind”) + -i (nisba suffix).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish اقربا, from Arabic اَقْرِبَاء (aqribāʔ, “relatives”), plural of قَرِيب (qarīb, “relative, relation”).
From Ottoman Turkish اقران (akran), from Arabic أَقْرَان (ʔaqrān).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عقرب (ʼakreb, “scorpion”), from Arabic عَقْرَب (ʕaqrab).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عكسی (aksi), from Arabic عَكْس (ʕaks). By surface analysis, akis + -i.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish اقطار (aktâr), from earlier Ottoman Turkish عطار, from Arabic عَطَّار (ʕaṭṭār).
From Ottoman Turkish عاقبت (akıbet), from Arabic عَاقِبَة (ʕāqiba).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عقل (akl), from Arabic عَقْل (ʕaql).
From Ottoman Turkish علاقه (alaka), from Arabic عَلاقَة (ʕalāqa).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish علامت (alamet), from Arabic عَلَامَة (ʕalāma).
From Ottoman Turkish علی العجله, from Arabic عَلَى الْعَجَلَة (ʕalā al-ʕajala).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish علی العاده (ʿalâ'l-ʿâde), Arabic عَلَى الْعَادَة (ʕalā al-ʕāda).
From Ottoman Turkish علی العموم, from Arabic عَلَى (ʕalā) and الْعُمُوم (al-ʕumūm). Compare Azerbaijani ələlümum, Persian علیالعموم (“alalomum”).
From Ottoman Turkish علم (alem), from Arabic عَلَم (ʕalam).
From Ottoman Turkish علناً (alenen), from Arabic عَلَنًا (ʕalanan), adverbial accusative of عَلَن (ʕalan).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish علنی, from Arabic عَلَنِيّ (ʕalaniyy, “public”).
From Ottoman Turkish آلت (alet), from Arabic آلَة (ʔāla).

parole.significato: Being in opposition, contrariness or detriment to or of someone or something.
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish علیه (ʿaleyh), from Arabic عَلَيْهِ (ʕalayhi, “upon him”), form of عَلَى (ʕalā).
From Arabic عَلَيْهَا السَّلَامُ (ʕalayhā s-salāmu).

parole.significato: blessings and peace be upon him
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish علیه الصلات والسلام (aleyhi s-salâtü ve-s-selâm), from Arabic عَلَيْهِ ٱلصَّلَاةُ وَٱلسَّلَامُ (ʕalayhi ṣ-ṣalātu was-salāmu).
From Arabic عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ (ʕalayhi s-salāmu).
From Ottoman Turkish علیكم سلام (aleyküm selam), from Arabic وَعَلَيْكُمُ ٱلسَّلَامُ (waʕalaykumu s-salāmu).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish علیل (alîl), from Arabic عَلِيل (ʕalīl).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish علی الاعلی (’aliyyü l-a’lâ), from Arabic عَلِيُّ الأَعْلَى (ʕaliyyu al-ʔaʕlā)
Ultimately a calque of Arabic الشُّكْرُ لِلّٰهِ (aš-šukru lillāhi, “thank God”, literally “gratitude to God”).

parole.significato: Allahu akbar (God is the most great)
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish الله اكبر, from Arabic اَللَّٰهُ أَكْبَرُ (allāhu ʔakbaru).

parole.significato: One who is very learned, who has extensive knowledge.
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish علامه (ʿallāme, “exceedingly learned, well versed in genealogies”), from Arabic عَلَّامة (ʕallāma).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish اما (ammâ), from Arabic أَمَّا (ʔammā). Doublet of amma.
From Ottoman Turkish امان (amân), from Arabic أَمَان (ʔamān, “tranquillity, peacefulness”).

parole.significato: deed, an action in the context of religious morality
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عمل ('amel), from Arabic عَمَل (ʕamal).
From Ottoman Turkish عمله (amele, “workers; government officials”), from Arabic عَمَلَة (ʕamala), plural of عَامِل (ʕāmil, “worker, laborer”).
From Ottoman Turkish عملیات, from Arabic عَمَلِيَّات (ʕamaliyyāt), plural of عَمَلِيَّة (ʕamaliyya). Doublet of ameliye.
From Ottoman Turkish عملیه (ameliye), from Arabic عَمَلِيَّة (ʕamaliyya). Doublet of ameliyat (“operation, surgery”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عامل (‘âmil), from Arabic عَامِل (ʕāmil),
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish آمر, from Arabic آمِر (ʔāmir).
From Arabic آمِر (ʔāmir) and Persian ـانه (-âne).

Inherited from Ottoman Turkish آن (ân), from Arabic آن (ʔān).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عنعنه (anane), from Arabic عَنْعَنَة (ʕanʕana).

parole.significato: anise, an umbelliferous plant of the species Pimpinella anisum and the liqueur made from its seeds
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish آناصون (anason, “anise”), from Old Anatolian Turkish [Term?], from Arabic أَنِيسُون (ʔanīsūn, “anise”), from Ancient Greek ἄνισον (ánison), ultimately from Egyptian jnst.

parole.significato: sudden (happening quickly and with little or no warning)
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish آنی, from Arabic آنِيّ (ʔāniyy, “timely, present”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish ابدال (abdal, aptal), from Arabic أَبْدَال pl (ʔabdāl). Doublet of abdal.
From Ottoman Turkish عار (ar), from Arabic عَار (ʕār).

parole.significato: A'raf, a limbo realm between Heaven and Hell inhabited by those whose sins and virtues are evenly balanced.
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish اعراف (araf), from Arabic أَعْرَاف (ʔaʕrāf), plural of عُرْف (ʕurf, “crest, height”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish اراضی (arazi), from Arabic أَرَاضٍ (ʔarāḍin), plural of أَرْض (ʔarḍ).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish ﻋﺮﺑﺪﻩ (arbede), from Arabic عَرْبَدَة (ʕarbada).
From Ottoman Turkish عارف (ârif), from Arabic عَارِف (ʕārif).
From Ottoman Turkish عرفه (ʿarife), from Arabic عَرَفَة (ʕarafa).
From Ottoman Turkish عرصه (arsa), from Arabic عَرْصَة (ʕarṣa).
From Ottoman Turkish ارض (arz), from Arabic أَرْض (ʔarḍ), from Proto-Semitic *ʔarṣ́-.
From Ottoman Turkish عرض (arz), from Arabic عَرْض (ʕarḍ).
From Ottoman Turkish عارضه (arıza), from Arabic عَارِضَة (ʕāriḍa), feminine of عَارِض (ʕāriḍ).

parole.significato: the highest rank of the sky, heaven
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عرش (ʿarş), from Arabic عَرْش (ʕarš).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عصا, from Arabic عَصَا (ʕaṣā)
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عصبی, from Arabic عَصَبِي (ʕaṣabī)
From Ottoman Turkish اصالت (asâlet), from Arabic أَصَالَة (ʔaṣāla).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عصب, from Arabic عَصَب (ʕaṣab)
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish اصغری (asgari), from Arabic أَصْغَر (ʔaṣḡar).
From Ottoman Turkish عاصی, from Arabic عَاصٍ (ʕāṣin).
From Ottoman Turkish عصیده, from Arabic عَصِيدَة (ʕaṣīda).
From Ottoman Turkish اصیل (“rooted, sound, noble”), from Arabic أَصِيل (ʔaṣīl).

parole.significato: soldier (any member of a military, regardless of specialty or rank)
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عسكر (ʼasker)), from Arabic عَسْكَر (ʕaskar, “army”), from Persian لشکر (laškar, “army”). Displaced Turkish çeri.
From Ottoman Turkish عسكری (askeri), from Arabic عَسْكَرِيّ (ʕaskariyy), from عَسْكَر (ʕaskar, “soldiers, army”), from an Iranian language. By surface analysis, asker + -i (nisba suffix).

parole.significato: never (as a matter of principle or intent; compare hiç)
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish اصلا, from Arabic أَصْلًا (ʔaṣlan). Doublet of aslen.

parole.significato: originally (as it was in the beginning)
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish اصلاً (aslen), from Arabic أَصْلًا (ʔaṣlan). By surface analysis, asıl (“origin”) + -en. Doublet of asla.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish اصلی (aslî), from Arabic أَصْلِيّ (ʔaṣliyy). By surface analysis, asıl (“origin”) + -i (nisba suffix).

parole.significato: safflower, bastard saffron, any cultivated, thistle-like plant of the species Carthamus tinctorius
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish آصپور (aspur), from Arabic عُصْفُر (ʕuṣfur, “safflower”).
From Arabic عَصْرِيّ (ʕaṣriyy).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish آصل, borrowed from Arabic أَصْل (ʔaṣl).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عصر (asr, asır), borrowed from Arabic عَصْر (ʕaṣr).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish اطلس (atlas), from Arabic أَطْلَس (ʔaṭlas)
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عطف, from Arabic عَطْف (ʕaṭf).
From Arabic عَاطِل (ʕāṭil).

parole.significato: stupidly, emptily, like a stuck pig
parole.testo: Reduplication of aval, from Ottoman Turkish احول, from Arabic أَحْوَل (ʔaḥwal). Compare avel, from the same etymon.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عوام (avâm), from Arabic عَوَامّ (ʕawāmm).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish احول, from Arabic أَحْوَل (ʔaḥwal). Doublet of aval.
From Ottoman Turkish عورت, ultimately from Arabic عَوْرَة (ʕawra) possibly with contamination from Ottoman Turkish اراغت (urağut, “woman”). Doublet of avret and averaj.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عیال, from Arabic عِيَال (ʕiyāl).
From Ottoman Turkish عیان (ayân), from Arabic عِيَان (ʕiyān).
From Ottoman Turkish عیار (iyar, ayar, “setting”), from Arabic عِيَار (ʕiyār).
From Ottoman Turkish آیت (ayet), from Arabic آيَة (ʔāya).

parole.significato: Letter of the Arabic alphabet: ع
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عین (ayn), from Arabic عَين.

Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عيناً (ʿaynen, “by eye, by sight, exactly, without difference”), from Arabic عَيْنًا (ʕaynan), adverbial accusative of عَيْن (ʕayn, “eye”). By surface analysis, aynı (“same”) + -en. Compare Azerbaijani eynən (“exactly”), Uzbek aynan (“exactly”) and Uyghur ئەينەن (eynen
From Ottoman Turkish عیواض, from Arabic عِيوَاض (ʕīwāḍ), alteration of عِوَض (ʕiwaḍ).

Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عیاش (ʿayyaş, “fond of good living and merriment, a toper, sot”), from Arabic عَيَّاشْ (ʕayyāš, “one who lives in prosperity”), from عَاشَ (ʕāša, “to live, to be alive”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عیب (ʿayb), from Arabic عَيْب (ʕayb).

parole.significato: chaste tree, monk's pepper, a shrub of the species Vitex agnus-castus, native to the Mediterranean basin
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish آید (ayıd, “chaste tree”), perhaps from Arabic حَائِط (ḥāʔiṭ, “wall”) according to Nishanyan.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish اعضا (aza), from Arabic أَعْضَاء (ʔaʕḍāʔ), plural of عُضْو (ʕuḍw). An originally plural form reinterpreted as singular.
From Ottoman Turkish عظمت (azamet), from Arabic عَظَمَة (ʕaẓama).
From Ottoman Turkish اعظم (azam), from Arabic أَعْظَم (ʔaʕẓam, “greatest”). The final vowel is a 20th century Turkish addition.

From Ottoman Turkish عذاب (azāb, “pain, torment, torture”), from Arabic عَذَاب (ʕaḏāb). An early Turkic borrowing akin to Karakhanid [script needed] (ˁaẕāb), Bashkir ғазап (ğazap), Kazakh азап (azap), Kyrgyz азап (azap), Tatar газап (ğazap), Uzbek azob.
From Ottoman Turkish عزل (ʿazl), from Arabic عَزْل (ʕazl).
From Ottoman Turkish عزم ('azm), from Arabic عَزْم (ʕazm).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عزیمت (azimet), from Arabic عَزِيمَة (ʕazīma).

parole.significato: rent paid for the pasture of a field after its crop has been gathered.
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish عزیر (ʿazir), from Arabic عَزِير (ʕazīr).
From Ottoman Turkish عزیز (aziz, “powerful, great; precious; beloved”), from Arabic عَزِيز (ʕazīz).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish اغیار (ağyar), from Arabic أَغْيَار (ʔaḡyār), plural of غَيْر (ḡayr) (whence gayr and gayri-). Compare Azerbaijani əğyar.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عشیرت (aşiret), from Arabic عَشِيرَةٌ (ʕašīratun).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عشق ('aşk), from Old Anatolian Turkish عشق (ʼeşq) from Arabic عِشْق (ʕišq).

parole.significato: a special Turkish dessert eaten all year round but especially in Ashura
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish عاشورا, عاشوره, from Arabic عَاشُورَاء (ʕāšūrāʔ).

parole.significato: a dangerous situation that arises suddenly, an unexpected peril, calamity, affliction
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بادره, from Arabic بَادِرَة (bādira).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بهار (bahâr), from Arabic بَهَار (bahār, “spice”), from Classical Persian بَهَار (bahār, “blossom”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بهارات, from Arabic بَهَارَات (bahārāt), plural of بَهَار (bahār).
From Ottoman Turkish بحث (bahs), from Arabic بَحْث (baḥṯ, “search, investigation; report, discussion”). The modern senses developed in Ottoman Turkish.
From Ottoman Turkish بهری, from Arabic بَحْرِيّ (baḥriyy). Compare Maltese baħri.
Calque of Arabic ناظِر (nāẓir), coined during the language reform. By surface analysis, bak- + -an. Displaced nazır, also from the same etymon.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish باقی (bâki), from Arabic بَاقٍ (bāqin, “eternal”).
From Arabic بَاكِر (bākir).
From Ottoman Turkish باكره (bakire), from Arabic بَاكِرَة (bākira).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بقال (bakkal, “greengrocer; grocer”), from Arabic بَقَّال (baqqāl), with semantic narrowing.

parole.significato: broad bean, any edible bean of the species Vicia faba, widely cultivated as a crop
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish باقلا (bakla, “broad bean”), from Arabic بَاقِلّاء (bāqillāʔ, “broad bean”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بلغم (balgam), from Arabic بَلْغَم (balḡam), ultimately from Ancient Greek φλέγμα (phlégma, “phlegm”).
From Ottoman Turkish بالغ (baliğ), from Arabic بَالِغ (bāliḡ), from بَلَغَ (balaḡa, “to arrive at; to reach puberty”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish باب (bâb), borrowed from Arabic بَاب (bāb), borrowed from Aramaic בָּבָא, borrowed from Akkadian bābum.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish ﺑﺮﺹ (baras), from Arabic بَرَص (baraṣ, “leprosy”).
From Ottoman Turkish بارز (bariz), from Arabic بَارِز (bāriz).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish باروت (barut, “gunpowder”), from Arabic بَارُود (bārūd, “saltpetre; gunpowder”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بصیرت (basîret), from Arabic بَصِيرَة (baṣīra).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بسیط (basît), from Arabic بَسِيط (basīṭ).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish باسور (basur), from Arabic بَاسُور (bāsūr), from Classical Syriac *ܒܳܨܘܿܪܴܐ (bāṣōrā, “sore, ulcer”).
From Ottoman Turkish بطانیه (battaniye), from Arabic بَطَّانِيَّة (baṭṭāniyya).
From Ottoman Turkish باطل (bâtıl), from Arabic بَاطِل (bāṭil).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بطن (batın), from Arabic بَطْن (baṭn).
From Ottoman Turkish بایات (bayat), from Arabic بَائِت (bāʔit).
From Ottoman Turkish بایع (bayiʼ), from Arabic بَائِع (bāʔiʕ).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بیطار (baytar, “veterinarian; farrier”), itself from Arabic بَيْطَار (bayṭār, “veterinarian, farrier”).
From Ottoman Turkish بعضا, from Arabic بَعْضًا (baʕḍan).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بدل, from Arabic بَدَل (badal, “substitution, equivalent”).

parole.significato: with one's body, bodily, in person, physically
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بدناً (bedenen), from Arabic بَدَنًا (badanan) adverbial accusative of بَدَن (badan, “body”). By surface analysis, beden (“body”) + -en.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بدنی (bedenî), from Arabic بَدَنِيّ (badaniyy). By surface analysis, beden (“body”) + -i (nisba suffix).
From Ottoman Turkish بدوی, from Arabic بَدَوِيّ (badawiyy).

parole.significato: pertaining to the science of embellishment in rhetoric
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish بدیعی (bedii), from Arabic بَدِيعِيّ (badīʕiyy).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بدیعیات (bediiyat), from Arabic بَدِيعِيَّات (badīʕiyyāt).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بدر, from Arabic بَدْر (badr).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بهیمیت (behimiyet, “bestiality”), from Arabic بَهِيمِيّة (bahīmiyya, “bestiality”).
From Ottoman Turkish بقا (beka), from Arabic بَقَاء (baqāʔ).

Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بكار (bekâr, “bachelor”), from Arabic بِكْر (bikr, “virgin”). Historically confused with the homophone بیكار (bekâr, “unemployed”), from Classical Persian بیکَار (bēkār).
From Ottoman Turkish بكارت (bekaret), from Arabic بَكَارَة (bakāra).
From Ottoman Turkish بلا (belâ), from Arabic بَلَاء (balāʔ, “affliction”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بلاغت (belâğat), from Arabic بَلَاغَة (balāḡa).
From Ottoman Turkish بلده (belde), from Arabic بَلْدَة (balda).
From Ottoman Turkish بلدیه (belediye), from Arabic بَلَدِيَّة (baladiyya).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بركت (bereket), from Arabic بَرَكَة (baraka, “blessing”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish برق (berḳ), from Arabic بَرْق (barq).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish برّاق (berrâk), from Arabic بَرَّاق (barrāq) meaning "shining, bright, clear".
From Ottoman Turkish بری, from Arabic بَرِّيّ (barriyy).

parole.significato: utterance of the bismillah; the respective formula itself; basmala.
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بسمله (besmele), borrowed from Arabic بَسْمَلَة (basmala).
From Ottoman Turkish بیان, from Arabic بَيَان (bayān). Compare Bengali বয়ান (boẏan).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بیانات (beyanat), from Arabic بَيَانَات (bayānāt).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بیاض (beyâz, “white”), from Arabic بَياض (bayāḍ, “whiteness, something white”).

parole.significato: bayt; a verse of classical Arabic, Persian, Turkic or Urdu poetry (similar to couplet)
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بیت (beyt), from Arabic بَيْت (bayt).

From Ottoman Turkish بین الملل (beyn-elmilel), from Arabic بَيْنَ ٱلْمِلَلِ (bayna l-milali, “between the nations”) with the word مِلّة (milla) in the uncommon or dated sense “people, nation”, which is current in Turkish millet. Compare Persian بینالمللی (beyna-lmelali). In Arabic itself, the word د
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بیت المال (beyt ül-mal), from Arabic بَيْت الْمَال (bayt al-māl).

From Ottoman Turkish بز (bez); see there for more. The ultimate origin is Arabic بَزّ (bazz), however, an influence from Byzantine Greek βύσσος (bússos) has been postulated in order to explain the mismatch in the vowels.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بشارت (beşâret), from Arabic بِشَارَة (bišāra).
From Ottoman Turkish بشر (beşer), from Arabic بَشَر (bašar).
From Ottoman Turkish ﺑﺸﺮﻯ (beşeri, “mankind; human”), from Old Anatolian Turkish ﺑﺸﺮﻯ, from Arabic بَشَرِيّ (bašariyy). By surface analysis, beşer (“human”) + -i (nisba suffix).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بیعت (bey'at), from Arabic بَيْعَة (bayʕa).

parole.significato: bid'a. A thing newly created or introduced, a creation, an invention, an innovation especially an innovation in religio…
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بدعت (bidʿat), derived from Arabic بِدْعَة (bidʕa).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بدایت (bidâyet), from Arabic بِدَايَة (bidāya).
From Arabic بِكْر (bikr)

From Ottoman Turkish بلاقید و شرط, from Arabic بِلَا (bilā, “without”), قَيْد (qayd, “restraint”), شَرْط (šarṭ, “condition”). Appeared as a set phrase c. 1920. In modern use replaced by kayıtsız şartsız.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بالعكس (bilʿaks, bilʿakis, “on the contrary”), from Arabic بِالْعَكْس (bi-l-ʕaks), from بِـ (bi-) + اَلْ (al-) + عَكْس (ʕaks), equivalent to bil- + akis (“reflection”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بلجمله (bilcümle), from Arabic بِالْجُمْلَة (bi-l-jumla), from بِـ (bi-) + اَلْ (al-) + جُمْلَة (jumla), equivalent to bil- + cümle (“all, everybody; sentence”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بالفعل (bilfiʿl), from Arabic بِٱلْفِعْلِ (bi-l-fiʕli), from بِـ (bi-) + اَلْ (al-) + فِعْل (fiʕl), equivalent to bil- + fiil (“work, deed, action, verb”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بالخاصه (bilhassa), from Arabic بِالْخَاصَّة (bi-l-ḵāṣṣa), from بِـ (bi-) + اَلْ (al-) + خَاصَّة (ḵāṣṣa), equivalent to bil- + hassa (“specialty, feature”).

Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بللور (billur), borrowed from Arabic بِلَّوْر (billawr), borrowed from Classical Persian بِلّور (billōr), from Middle Persian bylwl (/⁠*bēlūr⁠/), borrowed from Pali veḷuriya, from Proto-Dravidian *weḷ-ūr (name of a city) + Pali -iya.

Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بالمقابله (bilʿmuḳābele, “in return, reciprocally”), from Arabic بِالْمُقَابَلَة (bi-l-muqābala), from بِـ (bi-) + اَلْ (al-) + مُقَابَلَة (muqābala), equivalent to bil- + mukabele (“an act of responding, reciprocating”).
From Ottoman Turkish بنا (bina), from Arabic بِنَاء (bināʔ, “building, construction”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بناءً, from Arabic بِنَاءً (bināʔan), adverbial accusative of بِنَاء (bināʔ). By surface analysis, bina + -en (adverbial suffix).
From Ottoman Turkish بناءً علیه (binaen aleyh), from Arabic بِنَاءً عَلَيْهِ (bināʔan ʕalayhi).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بسم الله, from Arabic بِسْمِ اللّٰه (bismi llāh).

parole.significato: in the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful (the basmala)
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بسم الله الرحمن الرحیم, from Arabic بِسْمِ ٱللّٰهِ ٱلرَّحْمٰنِ ٱلرَّحِيمِ (bismi llāhi r-raḥmāni r-raḥīmi).

parole.significato: personally, in person, on one's own
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بالذات (biẕẕat), from Arabic بِالذَّات (bi-ḏ-ḏāt), from بِـ (bi-) + اَلْ (al-) + ذَات (ḏāt), equivalent to biz- + zat (“person”).

Coined by Turkish founding father Mustafa Kemal Atatürk. Phono-semantic matching of Arabic بُعْد (buʕd), which it displaced, morphologically boy (“length, size”) + -ut, from Proto-Turkic *bod (“body, stature, length”).

From Ottoman Turkish بدلا (budala), from Arabic اَبْدَال pl (abdāl) of singular بديل, بَدَل (badal, “a substitute; a good, religious man; saint”), بَدَل (badal, “a substitute; a good, religious man; saint”), from بَدَلَ (badala, “to replace”).
From Ottoman Turkish بخار (buhar), from Arabic بخار (buḵār).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بحران (buhrân), from Arabic بُحْرَان (buḥrān).
From Ottoman Turkish بحرانلی, from Arabic بُحْرَان (buḥrān). Equivalent to buhran (“crisis”) + -lı.

parole.significato: incense, biotic material that releases fragrant smoke when burnt, often used in religious rites
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بخور (buhur, bahur, “incense”), from Arabic بَخُور (baḵūr, “incense”).

parole.significato: chameleon, a reptile of the family Chamaeleonidae, able to change color and project its long tongue
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بوقلمون (bukalemun), from Arabic أَبُوقَلَمُون (ʔabūqalamūn), ultimately from Ancient Greek ὑποκάλαμον (hupokálamon).
From Ottoman Turkish بورغول (burğul), بلغور (bulğur), from Arabic بُرْغُل (burḡul).

Inherited from Ottoman Turkish برج (burc, “zodiac, constellation, tower”), from Arabic بُرْج (burj), from Classical Syriac ܒܘܪܓܐ (burgāʾ, “tower, columbarium”), from Ancient Greek πύργος (púrgos) or Latin burgus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerǵʰ- (“high”) (compare English borough).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بطلان, from Arabic ْبُطْلَان (buṭlān).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish باطنی (bâtınî), from Arabic بَاطِنِيّ (bāṭiniyy). By surface analysis, batın (“inward”) + -i (nisba suffix).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بهتان (bühtân), from Arabic بُهْتَان (buhtān, “false accusation”).
From Ottoman Turkish بلوغ (büluğ), from Arabic بُلُوغ (bulūḡ).
From childish talk, or derivated from Arabic بلوغ (bulūḡ, “puberty, maturity”). Compare English bollock, and Old Norse böllur.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish بنیه, from Arabic بُنْيَة (bunya).
From Ottoman Turkish بظر, from Arabic بَظْر (baẓr).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جاهل (cahil, “ignorant, stupid”), from Arabic جَاهِل (jāhil).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جاهلیه (cahiliye), from Arabic جَاهِلِيَّة (jāhiliyya).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جاهلیت (cahiliyet), from Arabic جَاهِلِيَّة (jāhiliyya).
From Ottoman Turkish جامع (cami'), from Arabic جَامِع (jāmiʕ, “congregational mosque”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جاموس (camus), from Arabic جَامُوس (jāmūs), from Classical Persian گَامیش (gāmēš). Doublet of kömüş and camış.
From Ottoman Turkish جانب (canib), from Arabic جَانِب (jānib).

Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جر اثقال (cerr-i eskâl, “jack, crane, derrick”), from Arabic جَرّ (jarr, “pulling, drawing, dragging”) + أَثْقَال (ʔaṯqāl), plural of ثِقْل (ṯiql, “weight, burden, load”).
From Ottoman Turkish جاری (cari), from Arabic جَارِي (jārī).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جاریه (câriye), from Arabic جَارِيَة (jāriya).
From Ottoman Turkish جاسوس (casus), from Arabic جَاسُوس (jāsūs).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جاذبه (cāẕibe), from Arabic جَاذِبَة (jāḏiba).

Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جاذب (cāzib, “that draws to itself, that attracts, attractive”), from Arabic جَاذِب (jāḏib, “attractive”), active participle of جَذَبَ (jaḏaba, “to attract, to captivate”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جبار (cebbâr), from Arabic جَبَّار (jabbār).
From Ottoman Turkish جبل (cebel, “mountain”), from Arabic جَبَل (jabal).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جبر (cebr), from Arabic جَبْر (jabr).
From Ottoman Turkish جبراً, from Arabic جَبْرًا (jabran), adverbial accusative of جَبْر (jabr). Formally, the Arabic accusative of cebir. By surface analysis, cebir (“compulsion”) + -en.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جبری (cebrî), from Arabic جَبْرِيّ (jabriyy). By surface analysis, cebir (“compulsion”) + -i (nisba suffix). Compare Azerbaijani cəbri.
From Ottoman Turkish جفا (cefâ), from Arabic جَفَاء (jafāʔ, “cruelty, oppression”), verbal noun of Arabic جَفَا (jafā, “to be crude, to be harsh”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جهالت, from Arabic جَهَالَة (jahāla).

Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جهنم (cehennem), from Old Anatolian Turkish جهنم (cehennem), from Arabic جَهَنَّم (jahannam), from Hebrew גֵּיהִנּוֹם (gehinóm, “Gehenna”), from גַּיא בֶּן הִנֹּם (Ge ben Hinnom, “Valley of Hinnom”).
From Arabic جَلَادَة (jalāda).
From Ottoman Turkish جلال (celal), from Arabic جَلَال (jalāl).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جلیل (celil), from Arabic جَلِيل (jalīl).
From Ottoman Turkish جلاد (cellad), from Arabic جَلَّاد (jallād).
From Ottoman Turkish جلب (celb), from Arabic جَلْب (jalb), verbal noun of Arabic جَلَبَ (jalaba, “to fetch”). Cognate with Azerbaijani cəlb.
From Ottoman Turkish جلسه (celse), from Arabic جَلْسَة (jalsa). Compare Azerbaijani cələsə and Persian جلسه (jalase), both of which have an additional vowel.
From Ottoman Turkish جماعت (cema'at), from Arabic جَمَاعَة (jamāʕa).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جمعیت (cemʼiyet), from Arabic جَمْعِيَّة (jamʕiyya).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جنابت (cenâbet), from Arabic جَنَابَة (janāba).
From Arabic جَنَاح (janāḥ).
From Ottoman Turkish جناب (cenab), from Arabic جَنَاب (janāb).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جنازه (cenâze, cinâze), from Arabic جَنَازَة (janāza).
From Ottoman Turkish جنوب (cenub, “south; south wind”), from Arabic جَنُوب (janūb).
From Ottoman Turkish جیب (ceb, cep), from Arabic جَيْب (jayb, “pocket”).
From Ottoman Turkish جبهه (cebhe), from Arabic جَبْهَة (jabha).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جراحت (cerâhat), from Arabic جِرَاحَة (jirāḥa).

parole.significato: gift of the gab, the skill or ability to talk eloquently, glibly, and convincingly
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جربزه (cerbeze), from Arabic جَرْبَزَة (jarbaza, “deception, swindle”), itself possibly from Classical Persian گربز (gorbez, “cunning”).

parole.significato: course, flow, current (of liquid, electricity, wind, events, etc.)
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish جریان (cereyan), from Arabic جَرَيَان (jarayān).

parole.significato: ledger used by tax collectors to record the surface areas of land during the Ottoman Empire
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جریده (ceride, “journal, newspaper”), from Arabic جَرِيدَة (jarīda, “detachment; newspaper”).
From Ottoman Turkish جراح (cerrah), from Arabic جَرَّاح (jarrāḥ).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جسارت (cesaret, “courage; impudence”), from Arabic جَسَارَة (jasāra), verbal noun of جَسَرَ (jasara).
From Ottoman Turkish جسد (cesed), from Arabic جَسَد (jasad).
From Ottoman Turkish جسور (cesur), from Arabic جَسُور (jasūr).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جد (cedd, cet, “a grandfather, one's ancestor”), from Arabic جَدّ (jadd, “grandfather, ancestor, glory”) from جَدَّ (jadda, “to be new, to be serious or earnest”).
From Ottoman Turkish جدول (cedvel), from Arabic جَدْوَل (jadwal).

parole.significato: as an answer, in reply to
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish جواباً (cevaben), from Arabic جَوَابًا (jawāban).
From Ottoman Turkish جواب (cevab), from Arabic جَوَاب (jawāb).

parole.significato: synonym of gezinme (“the act of wandering”)
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish جولان (cevelan), from Arabic جَوَلَان (jawalān).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جوهر (cevher), from Arabic جَوْهَر (jawhar), from Classical Persian گوهر (gawhar).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جوز (cevz), from Arabic جَوْز (jawz), from Middle Persian 𐭢𐭥𐭦 (gʿz /⁠gōz⁠/); see Old Armenian ընկոյզ (ənkoyz) for more.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جوال, from Arabic جَوَّال (jawwāl).
From Ottoman Turkish جزا (ceza), from Arabic جَزَاء (jazāʔ).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جزیره (cezire), borrowed from Arabic جَزِيرَة (jazīra).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جذب (cezb), from Arabic جَذْب (jaḏb).

parole.significato: jezve, a Turkish coffee pot with a long handle
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish جزوه (cezve), from Arabic جَذْوَة (jaḏwa) or جِذْوَة (jiḏwa, “ember”).
From Ottoman Turkish جبلیت, borrowed from Arabic جِبِلِّيَّة (jibilliyya).
From Ottoman Turkish جداً (cidden), from Arabic جِدًّا (jiddan).

parole.significato: serious (without humor or expression of happiness)
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish جدی (ciddi, “earnest, strenuous; serious”), from Arabic جِدِّيّ (jiddiyy).

Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جدیت (ciddiyet, “seriousness, severity, solemnity”), from Arabic جِدِّيَّة (jiddiyya), from جِدِّيّ (jiddiyy, “serious, grave, earnest”), from جَدَّ (jadda, “to be new, to be serious or earnest”).
From Ottoman Turkish جهاد (cihad, “struggle, effort; jihad”), from Arabic جِهَاد (jihād, “struggle; effort”).
From Ottoman Turkish جهاز (cihaz), from Arabic جِهَاز (jihāz). Doublet of çeyiz.
From Ottoman Turkish جهت (cihet), from Arabic جِهَة (jiha).

parole.significato: A mixture used to give shine to wooden, metallic, leather etc. objects; polish, luster.
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جلا (cilā, “a cleansing, furbishing, burnishing; brightness, gloss, luster, any substance or process that gives luster; a polish; a dispelling grief, anxiety”), from Arabic جَلَاء (jalāʔ), verbal noun of جَلَا (jalā, “to polish, to clear, to remove, to depart”).
From Ottoman Turkish جلد (cild), from Arabic جِلْد (jild), from Proto-Semitic *gild-.

parole.significato: A behavior meant to please or seem cute, flirtatious or coquettish attitude.
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جلوه (cilve, “a formally showing a bride to her husband after marriage, when he sees her unveiled for the first time, a present as due from a husband to his bride on first beholding her unveiled, (from the foregoing) the coy first appearance of a bride unveiled, coquet

parole.significato: Letter of the Arabic alphabet: ج
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جیم (cîm), from Arabic جِيم (jīm).
From Arabic جِمَاع (jimāʕ).
From Ottoman Turkish جن, from Arabic جِنّ (jinn).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جِنَائِيّ (cinai), from Arabic جِنَائِيّ (jināʔiyy).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جناس (cinas), from Arabic جِنَاس (jinās), verbal noun of جَانَسَ (jānasa, “to be related to, to be similar to”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جنایت (cinayet, “crime”), from Arabic جِنَايَة (jināya). Doublet of günah.
From Ottoman Turkish جنس, from Arabic جِنْس (jins). Doublet of janr.
From Ottoman Turkish جنسیت (cinsiyet), from Arabic جِنْسِيَّة (jinsiyya). By surface analysis, cins + -iyet.
From Ottoman Turkish جنسی (cinsi), from Arabic جِنْسِيّ (jinsiyy).

parole.significato: The game in which players on horseback throw javelins with blunted ends at their opponents to score points.
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish جرید (cerid, cirid, cirit, “stick, dart, javelin”), from Arabic جَرِيد (jarīd, “defoliated palm, javelin”). Cognates include Armenian ջիրիդ (ǰirid), Azerbaijani cirit, Bulgarian джирит (džirit), English jereed, Polish dziryt, Serbo-Croatian џирит.
From Arabic جِسْم (jism).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جسمانی (cismânî), from Arabic جِسْمَانِيّ (jismāniyy).
From Ottoman Turkish جوار (civar), from Arabic جِوَار (jiwār).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جزیه (cizye), from Arabic جِزْيَة (jizya).

parole.significato: geography (study of physical structure and inhabitants of the Earth)
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جغرافیا, from Arabic جُغْرَافِيَا (juḡrāfiyā), from Ancient Greek γεωγραφία (geōgraphía).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جمهور (cümhur, “public; republic; anarchy”), from Arabic جُمْهُور (jumhūr).

parole.significato: A robe worn by people of law or religion as well as university professors and students during their graduation; jubbah.
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جبه (cübbe, “an outer robe or gown, with full sleeves and long skirts, and open in front”), from Arabic جُبَّة (jubba).

parole.significato: accession to the throne, particularly in the Ottoman Empire
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جلوس (cülûs), from Arabic جُلُوس (julūs).
From Ottoman Turkish جمله, from Arabic جُمْلَة (jumla).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جملةً (cümleten), from Arabic جُمْلَةً (jumlatan) adverbial accusative of جُمْلَة (jumla, “series, whole range, collectivity”).

parole.significato: someone who has not purified themself through a special abdest after engaging in a sexual activity
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جنب, from Arabic جُنُب (junub).
From Ottoman Turkish جرأت (boldness, courage), from Arabic جُرْأَة (jurʔa).
From Ottoman Turkish جرم (cürm), from Arabic جُرْم (jurm).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جثه (cüsse), from Arabic جُثَّة (juṯṯa).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جزء (cüz’), from Arabic جُزْء (juzʔ).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جزئی (cüzî), from Arabic جُزْئِيّ (juzʔiyy).

parole.significato: leprosy, an infectious disease caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium leprae
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish جذام (cüzam, cüzzam), from Arabic جُذَام (juḏām, “leprosy”).

parole.significato: Letter of the Arabic alphabet: ض
parole.testo: From Arabic ضَاد (ḍād).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish دخل (dahl, “connection, revenue”), from Arabic دَخْل (daḵl). Doublet of tahıl.
From Ottoman Turkish دائما (daima), from Arabic دَائِمًا (dāʔiman), adverbial accusative of دَائِم (dāʔim). By surface analysis, daim + -en.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish دائر (da'ir, dayir), from Arabic دَائِر (dāʔir), active participle of دَارَ (dāra, “to revolve around”). Compare Kumyk даир (dair).

parole.significato: the inner part of a full circle
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish دائره (daire), from Arabic دَائِرَة (dāʔira).

parole.significato: precise (mostly used for timekeeping devices, hassas for other (mechanical or electronic devices)
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish دقیق (dakîk), from Arabic دَقِيق (daqīq).
From Ottoman Turkish دقیقه (dakika), from Arabic دَقِيقَة (daqīqa).

parole.significato: Letter of the Arabic alphabet: د
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish دال, from Arabic دَال (dāl).

From Ottoman Turkish ضلالت (dalalet, “being astray or lost; error”), from Arabic ضَلَالَة (ḍalāla), verbal noun of ضَلَّ (ḍalla, “to go astray; to lose”). The initial d is unusual; more often ض (ḍ) in Arabic becomes z when borrowed into in Turkish.
Derived from Arabic دَار (dār).
From Ottoman Turkish ضربه (zarbe), from Arabic ضَرْبَة (ḍarba).
From Arabic دَرْبُوكَة (darbūka).

Inherited from Ottoman Turkish ضرب (zarb, darb), from Arabic ضَرْب (ḍarb), note that the letter ض is pronounced exceptionally as the phoneme /d/ instead of the usual /z/ which is seen in the etymologically related mızrap (from مِضْرَاب (miḍrāb)) or zayıf (from ضَعِيف (ḍaʕīf)).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish دار الشفا (darüşşifa), from Arabic دَارُ ٱلشِّفَاء (dāru š-šifāʔ).
From Ottoman Turkish دعوی (dava), دعوا (dava) from Arabic دَعْوَى (daʕwā, “claim; lawsuit, process”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish دعوت (da'vet, “summons, invocation, invitation”), from Arabic دَعْوَة (daʕwa).

parole.significato: drum, a percussion instrument spanned with a thin covering, which forms an acoustic chamber
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish طاول (davul), variant of طبل (tabl), from Arabic طَبْل (ṭabl, “drum”), a word of Middle Iranian origin.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish دبدبه, from Arabic دبدبة (“heavy footsteps, the sound of horse hooves, the sound of drums”), a word of onomatopoeic origin.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish دجال, from Arabic دَجَّال (dajjāl), from Classical Syriac ܕܰܓܳܠܳܐ (daggālā, “liar”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish دفع (def’), from Arabic دَفْع (dafʕ).
From Ottoman Turkish دفعه (def'a), from Arabic دَفْعَة (dafʕa).

Inherited from Ottoman Turkish دفعةً (defʿaten), from Arabic دَفْعَةً (dafʕatan) adverbial accusative of دَفْعَة (dafʕa, “a push, thrust; one go; a payment”), from دَفَعَ (dafaʕa, “to push; to repel; to pay”).
From Ottoman Turkish دفن (defn), from Arabic دَفْن (dafn).
From Ottoman Turkish دفینه (define), from Arabic دَفِينَة (dafīna), from دَفَنَ (dafana, “to bury”).

parole.significato: Get out!, Beat it!, Piss off!
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish دفع اول (defʿ ol), from Arabic دَفْع (dafʕ), equivalent to def (“an act of pushing away, repelling, expelling”) + ol (“2nd P. Sg. positive imperative of olmak (“to be, to become”)”).

From Ottoman Turkish دفتر (defter), from Arabic دَفْتَر (daftar), from Aramaic דהפתּיר (defter), from Ancient Greek διφθέρα (diphthéra). Old Turkic [Term?] (/⁠tepter⁠/) is an early borrowing from Aramaic or Middle Persian. https://www.etimolojiturkce.com/kelime/defter
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish دها (deha), from Arabic دَهَاء (dahāʔ).
A pseudo-Arabic formation from Ottoman Turkish داخل (dahil) or دخیل (dahîl), from Arabic د خ ل (d ḵ l).

Inherited from Ottoman Turkish دهلیز (dehliz, dihliz), Arabic دِهْلِيز (dihlīz, “corridor, hallway”), itself from Persian دهلیز (dahliz, “vestibule, portico”), ultimately from Old Persian [Term?] (/⁠duvarθi-⁠/, “portico, colonnade”).
From Ottoman Turkish دهشت (dehşet), from Arabic دَهْشَة (dahša, “surprise, astonishment”).
From Ottoman Turkish دلالت (delalet), from Arabic دَلَالَة (dalāla).
From Ottoman Turkish دلیل (delil), from Arabic دَلِيل (dalīl).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish دم, from Arabic دَم (dam).
From Ottoman Turkish درجه (derece), from Arabic دَرَجَة (daraja).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish دراجه, from Arabic دراجة (darrāja).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish درس (ders), from Arabic دَرْس (dars).
From Ottoman Turkish دسیسه (desîse), from Arabic دَسِيسَة (dasīsa).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish دوا (deva), from Old Anatolian Turkish دوا (devā), from Arabic دَوَاء (dawāʔ).
From Ottoman Turkish دوام (devâm), from Arabic دَوَام (dawām).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish دوران (deverân), from Arabic دَوَرَان (dawarān).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish دور (devr), from Arabic دَوْر (dawr). Compare Turkmen döwür, Azerbaijani dövr, Kazakh дәуір (däwir).

Inherited from Ottoman Turkish دولت (devlet), from Old Anatolian Turkish دولت (devlet), from Arabic دَوْلَةٌ m sg (dawlatun, “a state”, indefinite nominative). Compare also Azerbaijani dövlət, Bashkir дәүләт (däwlät), Kazakh дәулет (däwlet), Kyrgyz дөөлөт (döölöt), Uzbek davlat, etc.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish دوران (devrân), from Arabic دَوَرَان (dawarān). Doublet of deveran.
From Ottoman Turkish دوره (devre), from Arabic دَوْرَة (dawra).

parole.significato: by way of transfer, with all fixtures included
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish دوراً (devren), from Arabic دَوْرًا (dawran) adverbial accusative of دَوْر (dawr, “turn, rotation”), verbal noun of دَارَ (dāra).
From Ottoman Turkish دوریه, feminine of دوری (“devri”), from Arabic دَوْرِيّ (dawriyy).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish دوری (devrî), from Arabic دَوْرِيّ (dawriyy). By surface analysis, devir (“cycle”) + -i (“nisba suffix”).

parole.significato: cuckold, wittol (A man who knows and tolerates his wife's infidelity with another man)
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish دیوث (deyyus), from Arabic دَيُّوث (dayyūṯ).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish دقت (dikkat), from Arabic دِقَّة (diqqa).

parole.significato: brain, the organ which controls the central nervous system
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish دماغ, borrowed from Arabic دِمَاغ (dimāḡ), a blend of دَم (dam) + مُخّ (muḵḵ).

parole.significato: System of beliefs dealing with soul, deity or life after death.
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish دین, from Arabic دِين (dīn) with some influence from Middle Persian (see the Arabic term for details).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish دیناً (dinen), from Arabic دِينًا (dīnan) adverbial accusative of دِين (dīn, “religion”).
From Ottoman Turkish درایت (dirâyet), from Arabic دِرَايَة (dirāya).
From Ottoman Turkish درهم (dirhem), from Arabic دِرْهَم (dirham), from Middle Persian 𐭦𐭥𐭦𐭭 (zʿzn), from Ancient Greek δραχμή (drakhmḗ). Doublet of drahma and drahoma.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish دیانت (diyânet), ultimately from Arabic دِيَانَة (diyāna).
From Ottoman Turkish دیار (diyar), from Arabic دِيَار (diyār), a plural form of دَار (dār).

parole.significato: diyya, a financial compensation paid to the victim or their heirs in cases of homicide, harm, damage, etc.
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish دیت (diyet), from Arabic دِيَة (diya, “bloodwite, wergeld”).

parole.significato: prayer (practice of communicating with one's God)
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish دعا (duʼâ) or دعاء (duʿā), from Arabic دُعَاء (duʕāʔ).
From Ottoman Turkish دخول (duhul, “entrance; consummation of marriage”), from Arabic دُخُول (duḵūl).
From Arabic دُمُور (dumūr).
From Ottoman Turkish داهی, from Arabic دَاهٍ (dāhin, “smart, cunning, resourceful”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish داخل (dahil, “who enters or is inside; inner, internal; inside, interior”), from Arabic دَاخِل (dāḵil), active participle of دَخَلَ (daḵala).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish داخلیه (dahiliyye, “interior”), from Arabic دَاخِلِيَّة (dāḵiliyya), from دَاخِل (dāḵil) + ـِيَّة (-iyya), active participle of دَخَلَ (daḵala, “to enter, to go in”).
From Ottoman Turkish داخلی (dâhilî), from Arabic دَاخِلِيّ (dāḵiliyy). By surface analysis, dâhil (“interior”) + -i (nisba suffix).

Inherited from Ottoman Turkish دكان (düḱḱan), from Arabic دُكَّان (dukkān), from Aramaic דּוּכָּנָא (dukkānā, “dais”), from Akkadian 𒆠𒍇 (/⁠dakkannu⁠/, “dais, platform, bench; niche, bedroom, private chambers or quarters”), from Sumerian 𒆠𒍇 (/⁠daggan⁠/, “chamber, doorway or its frame, niche in a wall
From Arabic دُلْدُل (duldul, “porcupine”), which is according to Islamic tradition also the name borne by a mule of the prophet Muhammad.
From Ottoman Turkish دنیا (dünya), from Arabic دُنْيَا (dunyā).
From Ottoman Turkish دنیوی (dünyevi), from Arabic دُنْيَوِيّ (dunyawiyy).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish دُسْتُور (düstur). Doublet of destur, borrowed directly from Classical Persian دَسْتُور (dastūr).

parole.significato: common swift, any small bird of the species Apus apus, that resembles a swallow or house martin
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish ابابیل (ebabil, “legendary birds mentioned in the Qur'an; Alpine swift”), from Arabic أَبَابِيل (ʔabābīl, “flocks”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish ابعاد (eb'âd), from Arabic أَبْعَاد (ʔabʕād), plural of Arabic بُعْد (buʕd, “dimension”).

parole.significato: abjad, a writing system for Arabic in which there is one glyph for each consonant, but vowels are not specified
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish ابجد (ebced), from Arabic أَبْجَد (ʔabjad, “abjad”), from the first four letters of the Arabic alphabet.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish ابدی (ebedî), from Arabic أَبَدِيّ (ʔabadiyy).

Inherited from Ottoman Turkish ابدیاً (ebediyyen), from Arabic أَبَدِيًّا (ʔabadiyyan) adverbial accusative of أَبَدِيّ (ʔabadiyy, “eternal”), from أَبَد (ʔabad, “eternity”) + ـِيّ (-iyy, nisba suffix).
From Ottoman Turkish ابدیت (ebediyet), from Arabic أَبَدِيَّة (ʔabadiyya).
From Ottoman Turkish ابدی (ebedî), from Arabic أَبَدِيّ (ʔabadiyy).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish ابد (ebed), from Arabic أَبَد (ʔabad).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish ابوین (“parents”), from Arabic أَبَوَيْنِ (ʔabawayni, “parents”), dual genitive/accusative of أَب (ʔab, “father”).
From Ottoman Turkish ابو, from Arabic أَبُو (ʔabū)

parole.significato: death, especially a natural one at the end of one’s lifespan
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish اجل (ecel), from Arabic أَجَل (ʔajal).
From Ottoman Turkish اجنبی, from Arabic أَجْنَبِيّ (ʔajnabiyy).
From Ottoman Turkish ادات (edât), from Arabic أَدَاة (ʔadāh).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish ادبیات (edebiyyât), ultimately from Arabic أَدَبِيَّات (ʔadabiyyāt). By surface analysis, edep + -iyat.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish ادبی (edebi), from Arabic أَدَبِيّ (ʔadabiyy). By surface analysis, edep + -i (nisba suffix).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish ادب (edeb), derived from Arabic أَدَب (ʔadab).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish ادوات (edevât), from Arabic أَدَوَات (ʔadawāt).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish افضل (efdal), from Arabic أَفْضَل (ʔafḍal).
From Ottoman Turkish افكار (efkâr), from Arabic أَفْكَار (ʔafkār), plural of فِكْر (fikr).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish افلاطون (eflatun), from Arabic أَفْلَاطُون (ʔaflāṭūn), from Ancient Greek Πλάτων (Plátōn), with semantic narrowing. Doublet of Eflatun.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish اهمیت (ehemmiyet), from Arabic أَهَمِّيَّة (ʔahammiyya).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish اهل (ehil), from Arabic أَهْل (ʔahl), from Proto-Semitic *ʔahl-.
From Ottoman Turkish اهل خبره (ehl-i hibre), from Arabic أَهْلُ الْخِبْرَةِ (ʔahlu l-ḵibrati).
From Ottoman Turkish اهلیت (ehliyyet), from Arabic أَهْلِيَّة (ʔahliyya). By surface analysis, ehl- + -iyet.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish اهلی, from Arabic أَهْلِيّ (ʔahliyy).
From Ottoman Turkish اهون (ehven), from Arabic أَهْوَن (ʔahwan).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish اكل ایتمك (ekl etmek), from Arabic أكل.
From Ottoman Turkish اكثر (ekser), from Arabic أَكْثَر (ʔakṯar).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish اكثریا (ekseriyyā), from Arabic أَكْثَرِيًّا (ʔakṯariyyan, “mostly, generally”), from أَكْثَر (ʔakṯar).
From Ottoman Turkish اكثریت (ekseriyet), from Arabic أَكْثَرِيَّة (ʔakṯariyya).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish اكثبه (eksibe), from Arabic أَكْثِبَة (ʔakṯiba), plural of كَثِيب (kaṯīb, “sand”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish اكابر (ekâbir), from Arabic أَكَابِر (ʔakābir).
From Ottoman Turkish البته (elbette), from Arabic اَلْبَتَّة (al-batta).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish البسه (elbise), from Arabic أَلْبِسَة (ʔalbisa), plural of Arabic لِبَاس (libās).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish الحمد لله, from Arabic اَلْحَمْدُ لِلّٰهِ (al-ḥamdu lillāhi, literally “praise [be] to God”).

parole.significato: Letter of the Arabic alphabet: ا
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish الف (elif), from Arabic أَلِف (ʔalif).
From Ottoman Turkish الیم (elim), from Arabic أَلِيم (ʔalīm).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish الوداع, borrowed from Arabic اَلْوَدَاع (al-wadāʕ). Doublet of veda.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish الزم (elzem), derived from Arabic أَلْزَم (ʔalzam).

parole.significato: trust, something trusted to another for safekeeping
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish امانت (emânet), from Arabic أَمَانَة (ʔamāna).

parole.significato: As a trust for safekeeping, on deposit
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish امانةً (emāneten), from Arabic أَمَانَةً (ʔamānatan) adverbial accusative of أَمَانَة (ʔamāna), verbal noun of أَمُنَ (ʔamuna).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish امارت (emâret), from Arabic إِمَارَة (ʔimāra).
From Ottoman Turkish امل (emel), from Arabic أَمَل (ʔamal).
From Ottoman Turkish امین (emin), from Arabic أَمِين (ʔamīn).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish املاك (emlak), from Arabic أَمْلَاك (ʔamlāk), plural of مِلْك (milk, “property, estate”).
From Arabic عَمّ (ʕamm).
From Ottoman Turkish امنیت, from Arabic أَمْنِيَّة (ʔamniyya).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish امر واقع (emr-i vakı), from Arabic أمر واقع (ʔamr wāqiʕ), from أمر (ʔamr, “matter, affair, concern”) + واقع (wāqiʕ, active participle of وَقَعَ (waqaʕa, “to happen”)).
From Ottoman Turkish امثال (emsal), plural of مثل (mesel), from Arabic مَثَل (maṯal). Formally, the Arabic plural of mesel.

Inherited from Ottoman Turkish امتعه (emtiaʿ), formerly plural of meta, from Ottoman Turkish متاع (mataʿ, “any organ or article of enjoyment, possession, or commerce”), from Arabic مَتَاع (matāʕ, “property, possessions”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish امیر, from Arabic أَمِيرْ (ʔamīr). Doublet of amiral.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish انانیت (enaniyyet), from Arabic أَنَانِيَّة (ʔanāniyya).
From Ottoman Turkish انایی (enayi), from Arabic أَنَا (ʔanā).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish اندر (ender), from Arabic أَنْدَر (ʔandar).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish انفس (enfes), from Arabic أَنْفَس (ʔanfas).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish انفسی (enfüsi), an Ottoman coinage from Arabic أَنْفُس (ʔanfus).
From Ottoman Turkish انقاض (enkâz), from Arabic أَنْقَاض (ʔanqāḍ), plural of نَقْض (naqḍ), verbal noun of نَقَضَ (naqaḍa, “to break, demolish”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish ارباب (erbab), from Arabic أَرْبَاب (ʔarbāb), plural of رَبّ (rabb) (whence Rab). Compare Azerbaijani ərbab.
From Ottoman Turkish اركان (erkân, “pillars; great men; tenets; general staff”), from Arabic أَرْكَان (ʔarkān).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish ارزاق (erzak), derived from Arabic أَرْزَاق (ʔarzāq), plural of رِزْق (rizq).

From Ottoman Turkish اسارت (esaret), from Arabic ء س ر (ʔ s r). Compare Crimean Tatar esaret, Azerbaijani əsarət, Uyghur ئاسارەت (asaret, “captivity”), Uzbek asorat (“captivity”) and Persian اسارت (“captivity”).
From Ottoman Turkish اساس, from Arabic أَسَاس (ʔasās).

parole.significato: from the beginning, from the foundation
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish اساساً (esāsen), from Arabic أَسَاسًا (ʔasāsan) adverbial accusative of أَسَاس (foundation, basis).
From Ottoman Turkish اسف (esef), from Arabic أَسَف (ʔasaf), verbal noun of أَسِفَ (ʔasifa).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish اثر (eser), from Arabic أَثَر (ʔaṯar), from Proto-Semitic *ʔaṯar-.

From Ottoman Turkish اسهام (esham), presuming a plural ***أَسْهَام (***ʔashām) of Arabic سَهْم (sahm), while in Arabic one uses, oddly contrary to this, the plural أَسْهُم (ʔashum) for “shares, stocks”, else verbal noun of form IV إِسْهَام (ʔishām, “to give a share in”).
From Ottoman Turkish اسیر (esir, “slave; prisoner”), from Arabic أَسِير (ʔasīr).
From Arabic أَثِير (ʔaṯīr).

parole.significato: having a rich olive skin tone; tan, tanned, dark
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish اسمر (esmer), from Arabic أَسْمَر (ʔasmar).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish اثنا (esna), from Arabic أَثْنَاء (ʔaṯnāʔ).
From Ottoman Turkish اصناف, from Arabic أَصْنَاف (ʔaṣnāf), plural of صِنْف (ṣinf).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish اصح (esahh), from Arabic أَصَحّ (ʔaṣaḥḥ). Elative of صَحِيح (ṣaḥīḥ, “true; right, correct”). Whence sahih.
From Ottoman Turkish استغفرالله (estağfurullah), from Arabic أَسْتَغْفِرُ اللَّٰه (ʔastaḡfiru llāh).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish اثواب (esvab), from Arabic أَثْوَاب (ʔaṯwāb), plural of Arabic ثَوْب (ṯawb).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish اطراف (etraf), from Arabic أَطْرَاف (ʔaṭrāf), plural of طَرَف (ṭaraf).
From Ottoman Turkish اوهام (evham), from Arabic أَوْهَام, plural of وَهْم (wahm).
From Ottoman Turkish اوقاف, from Arabic أَوْقَاف (ʔawqāf), plural of وَقْف (waqf, “inalienable property, waqf”) (from which vakıf).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish اولاد (evlâd), from Arabic أَوْلَاد (ʔawlād).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish اولیا (evliyâ, “saint, mahatma”), from Arabic أَوْلِيَاء (ʔawliyāʔ).
From Ottoman Turkish اوراق (evrak), from Arabic أَوْرَاق (ʔawrāq).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish اول, from Arabic أَوَّل (ʔawwal).

parole.significato: firstly, in the first place, first of all
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish اولا (evvela, “firstly, in the first place”), from Arabic أَوَّلًا (ʔawwalan).

parole.significato: eyalet (a former administrative division or province of the Ottoman Empire)
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish ایالت, borrowed from Arabic إِيَالَة (ʔiyāla).
From Ottoman Turkish ایلول (eylul), from Arabic أَيْلُول (ʔaylūl).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish اذان (ezân), derived from Arabic أَذَان (ʔaḏān, “call to prayer”).

parole.significato: eternity, time stretching back without beginning
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish ازل (ezel), from Arabic أَزَل (ʔazal).
From Ottoman Turkish اذیت, from Arabic أَذِيَّة (ʔaḏiyya). Cognate with Azerbaijani əziyyət, Uzbek aziyat.

parole.significato: Not permanent; temporary, used temporarily in place of another thing.
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish اكرتی, or ایرتی (eyreti, iyreti, “temporary, makeshift”), from Arabic عاريتي (“lent, borrowed, on loan; temporary”). Compare Persian عاریت.
From Ottoman Turkish اشقیا, from Arabic أَشْقِيَاء (ʔašqiyāʔ), plural of شَقِيّ (šaqiyy).

parole.significato: things, items, freight, goods; especially furnitures, white goods, trappings etc.
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish اشیا, from Arabic أَشْيَاء (ʔašyāʔ), plural of شَيْء (šayʔ). Formally, the Arabic plural of şey. Despite the etymology, and like other borrowings of broken plurals, it has developed its own Turkish plural form.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فعال (faʿʿâl), from Arabic فَعَّال (faʕʕāl).
From Ottoman Turkish فاجعه (fâciʿa), from Arabic فَاجِعَة (fājiʕa). Compare Azerbaijani faciə.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فاحشه (fahişe), from Arabic فَاحِشَة (fāḥiša). Compare Persian فاحشه for the meaning.

parole.significato: honorary (given as an honor, with no duties attached, and without payment)
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish فخری, from Arabic فَخْرِيّ (faḵriyy). Compare Azerbaijani fəxri.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فائق (fâik), from Arabic فَائِق (fāʔiq).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فاعل (fā'il), from Arabic فَاعِل (fāʕil).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فائض (faʼiz), from Arabic فَائِض (fāʔiḍ).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فقط (fakat), from Arabic فَقَط (faqaṭ).

Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فقیر (fakir), from Arabic فَقِير (faqīr). Cognate with Azerbaijani fağır (“poor”), Bashkir бахыр (baxır, “poor, miserable”), Kazakh пақыр (paqır, “poor, miserable”), Kyrgyz бакыр (bakır, “poor, miserable”), Turkmen pahyr (“poor thing”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فقر, from Arabic فَقْر (faqr).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فال (fal, “fortune telling”), from Arabic فَأْل (faʔl).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فلقه (falaka), from Arabic فَلَقَة (falaqa), ultimately from Ancient Greek φάλαγξ (phálanx).

parole.significato: the "you-know-" part in you-know-who or you-know-what
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فلان (falan), from Arabic فُلَان (fulān).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فانوس (fanus), from Arabic فَانُوس (fānūs), from Ancient Greek φανός (phanós, “lantern”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فرضا (farżā, faraża), from Arabic فَرْضًا (farḍan). By surface analysis, farz + -an.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فرضی, from Arabic فَرَضِيّ (faraḍiyy). By surface analysis, farz + -i. Compare Azerbaijani fərzi.
From Ottoman Turkish فرضیه (faraziye), from Arabic فَرَضِيَّة (faraḍiyya).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فراش (faraş), from Arabic فَرَّاش (farrāš), with semantic narrowing.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فاره (fare), from Arabic فَأْرَة (faʔra). Displaced Turkish sıçan. The computing sense is a semantic loan from English mouse.
From Ottoman Turkish فارق (farık), from Arabic فَارِق (fāriq).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فريضه (fariza), from Arabic فَرِيضَة (farīḍa).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فرق, from Arabic فَرْق (farq).
From Ottoman Turkish فرض (farz), from Arabic فَرْض (farḍ).
From Ottoman Turkish فصیح (fasih), from Arabic فَصِيح (faṣīḥ).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فصیله (fasile), from Arabic فَصِيلَة (faṣīla).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فَاسِق (fâsık), from Arabic فَاسِق (fāsiq).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فصل (faṣl), from Arabic فَصْل (faṣl).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فاصله (fâsıla), from Arabic فَاصِلَة (fāṣila).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فائده (faʼide), from Arabic فَائِدَة (fāʔida).
From Ottoman Turkish فضیلت, borrowed from Arabic فَضِيلَة (faḍīla).
From Ottoman Turkish فضله (fazla), from Arabic فَضْلَة (faḍla), from فَضَلَ (faḍala, “be left over, to excess”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فاضل (fazıl), from Arabic فَاضِل (fāḍil).
From Ottoman Turkish فجیع (feci), from Arabic فَجِيع (fajīʕ).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فجر (fecr), borrowed from Arabic فَجْر (fajr), from Proto-Semitic *pagr-.
From Ottoman Turkish فهم (fehm), from Arabic فَهْم (fahm).
From Ottoman Turkish فك (fekk), from Arabic فَكّ (fakk)
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فلك (felek), from Arabic فَلَك (falak).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فلسفه (felsefe), borrowed from Arabic فَلْسَفَة (falsafa), from فَلْسَفَ (falsafa), or possibly borrowed from Ancient Greek φιλοσοφία (philosophía).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فلسفی, from Arabic فَلْسَفِيّ (falsafiyy).

parole.significato: science (only referring to biology, chemistry, physics, and mathematics)
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فن (fen, “kind, variety; art, science”), from Arabic فَنّ (fann), ultimately from Classical Persian پَنْد (pand, “knack, trick”).
From Ottoman Turkish فنا, فناء (fena, “bad; sick; immoral; disagreeable”), from Arabic فَنَاء (fanāʔ).
From Ottoman Turkish فنی (fenni), from Arabic فَنِّيّ (fanniyy, “artistic”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فراغت (feragat), from Arabic فَرَاغ (farāḡ).

parole.significato: State of inner peace, serenity, contentment.
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فرح (ferah), from Arabic فَرَح (faraḥ).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فراست (feraset), from Arabic فِرَاسَة (firāsa).
Ottoman Turkish فردیت (ferdiyyet), from Arabic فَرْدِيَّة (fardiyya). Equivalent to fert (“individual”) + -iyet
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فردی (ferdî), from Arabic فَرْدِيّ (fardiyy). By surface analysis, fert (“individual”) + -i (nisba suffix).
From Ottoman Turkish فرسخ (fersah), from Arabic فَرْسَخ (farsaḵ).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فرد (ferd), from Arabic فَرْد (fard).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فصاحت (fesâhat), from Arabic فَصَاحَة (faṣāḥa).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فساد (fesâd), from Arabic فَسَاد (fasād).
From Ottoman Turkish فتح (feth), from Arabic فَتْح (fatḥ).

parole.significato: The interval between two prophets when there isn't a prophet alive; specifically the time between prophets Jesus and Mu…
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فترت (fetret), from Arabic فَتْرَة (fatra, “interval, interregnum”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فتان (fettan), from Arabic فَتَّان (fattān).
From Ottoman Turkish فتوی, from Arabic فَتْوَى (fatwā, “a decision given by a mufti”).
From Ottoman Turkish فوران (feverân), from Arabic فَوَرَان (fawarān), verbal noun of فَارَ (fāra, “to overflow, gush”).

From Ottoman Turkish فوق العاده, from Arabic فَوْق (fawq) and اَلْعَادَة (al-ʕāda), equivalent to fevk + âdet. Compare Azerbaijani fövqəladə, Crimean Tatar fevqulade, Uzbek favqulodda, Uyghur پەۋقۇلاددە (pewquladde) and Persian فوقالعاده.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فوري (fevrî), from Arabic فَوْرِيّ (fawriyy)
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فیضان (feyezan), from Arabic فَيَضَان (fayaḍān).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فضا (feza), from Arabic فَضَاء (faḍāʔ, “open area, empty space”).

parole.significato: at (often used with prices or dates)
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فی, from Arabic فِي (fī).
From Ottoman Turkish فدیه (fidye), from Arabic فِدْيَة (fidya).
From Ottoman Turkish فعل, from Arabic فِعْل (fiʕl).
From Ottoman Turkish فعلاً, from Arabic فِعْلًا (fiʕlan), from فِعْل (fiʕl).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فعلی (fiili), from Arabic فِعْلِيّ (fiʕliyy).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فكر (fikr, fikir), from Arabic فِكْر (fikr). Cognate with Azerbaijani fikir, Crimean Tatar fikir, Turkmen pikir

Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فكرا (fikren), from Arabic فِكْرًا (fikran), adverbial accusative of فِكْر (fikr, “thought”). By surface analysis, fikir (“thought”) + -en. Compare Azerbaijani fikrən and Uzbek fikran.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فكری (fikrî), from Arabic فِكْرِيّ (fikriyy). By surface analysis, fikir (“thought, idea”) + -î (nisba suffix).

parole.significato: elephant, a mammal of the order Proboscidea, having a large trunk
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فیل (fil, “elephant”), from Arabic فِيل (fīl), from Middle Persian pyl (/⁠pīl⁠/), ultimately from Akkadian 𒄠𒋛 (/⁠pīru⁠/).
From Ottoman Turkish فلوقه (fıluka, fılıka, füluka, filuka), فولوقه (fuluka), فلكه, فلیكه (filika), from Arabic فَلُوكَة (falūka), partially via Italian feluca, from Arabic فُلْك (fulk).
From Ottoman Turkish فلز (filizz, “mineral, metal”), from Arabic فِلِزّ (filizz).

Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فنجان (fincan), borrowed from Arabic فِنْجَان (finjān), borrowed from Classical Persian پِنْگَان (pingān), possibly borrowed from Classical Syriac ܦܝܢܟܐ (pīnəḵā), from Aramaic פִּינְכָא (pīnəkā), borrowed from Ancient Greek πίναξ (pínax).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فرار (firâr), borrowed from Arabic فِرَار (firār).
From Ottoman Turkish فراری (firari), from Arabic ف ر ر (f r r). Compare Persian فراری (farâri) from the same Arabic root.

Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فرعون (fir'avun), borrowed from Arabic فِرْعَوْن (firʕawn), possibly borrowed from Classical Syriac ܦܹܪܥܘܼܢ, borrowed from Koine Greek Φαραών (Pharaṓn), borrowed from Biblical Hebrew פַּרְעֹה, borrowed from Egyptian pr-ꜥꜣ, from pr + ꜥꜣ.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فردوس (firdevs), from Old Anatolian Turkish فردوس (firdevs), from Arabic فِرْدَوْس (firdaws, “paradise, Heaven”), ultimately from Proto-Iranian *paridayjah.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فی سبیل الله (fi sebili llah), from Arabic فِي سَبِيلِ ٱلله (fī sabīli llāh, “in the cause of God”). Compare Uzbek piysabillo (“wholeheartedly, sincerely”).
From Ottoman Turkish فتیل (fetil, fitil), from Arabic فَتِيل (fatīl).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فتنه (fitne), from Arabic فِتْنَة (fitna).

Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فیات (fiyat), فیئات (fiʼat, “price”). Pseudo-Arabism formed artificially in Ottoman by combining the Arabic plural ending ـَات (-āt) with فی (fi, “rate, price”), itself from dialectal Arabic فِي (fī, “in; about; times”).

parole.significato: kind of fine, white, wholemeal bread, which was mostly distributed to the poor in soup kitchens
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فودله (fodla), from Arabic فَضْلَة (faḍla). Doublet of fazla.
From Ottoman Turkish فحش, from Arabic فُحْش (fuḥš).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فقرا, from Arabic فُقَرَاء (fuqarāʔ), plural form of فَقِير (faqīr, “poor man, pauper”).

parole.significato: sweet mock orange, any flowering plant of the species Philadelphus coronarius, native to Caucasus
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فل (ful, “sweet mock orange”), from Arabic فِلّ (fill, “Arabian jasmine”).

parole.significato: broad bean, any edible bean of the species Vicia faba, widely cultivated as a crop
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فول (ful), from Arabic فُول (fūl, “fava bean”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فضولی (fużûli, “pertaining to excess; unjust”), from Arabic فُضُولِيّ (fuḍūliyy, “curious, prying”), from فُضُول (fuḍūl, “curiosity”) + ـِيّ (-iyy, nisba suffix).

parole.significato: a person who commits open sins and indulges in adultery
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فاجر (fâcir), from Arabic فَاجِر (fājir).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فانی (fânî), Old Anatolian Turkish فانی (fānī), borrowed from Arabic فَانِي (fānī).
From Ottoman Turkish فروع, borrowed from Arabic فُرُوع (furūʕ).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فتور (fütur, “abatement, becoming despirited, languor”), from Arabic فُتُور (futūr, “lukewarmness; languour, indifference”).
From Ottoman Turkish فقره (fıkra), from Arabic فِقْرة (fiqra, “short text, short story, line of a poem”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فقه (fıkh), from Arabic فِقْه (fiqh).
From Ottoman Turkish فرقه, from Arabic فِرْقَة (firqa).
According to Çağbayır, the same word as Turkish hırka (“cardigan”), from Arabic خِرْقَة (ḵirqa).
From Ottoman Turkish فرصت (fırsat), Arabic فُرْصَة (furṣa).

Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فسقیه (fıskiye), from Arabic فِسْقِيَّة (fisqiyya). According to Nishanyan, the word is derived from the onomatopoeic word fıs, fış (cfr. fışkırmak) with the addition of the suffix -iye, and hence the Arabic word would be derived from the Turkish one.

parole.significato: pistachio, the nutlike fruit produced by any tree in the species Pistacia vera
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فستق (fıstık), from Arabic فُسْتُق (fustuq), from Middle Persian pstk' (pistag).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فستقی (füstuḳî, fıstıḳî), from Arabic فُسْتُقِيّ (fustuqiyy). By surface analysis, fıstık + -i (nisba suffix).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فطرت, from Arabic فِطْرَة (fiṭra), from Ge'ez ፍጥረት (fəṭrät, “creation; nature, disposition”).

parole.significato: hernia (part of the body protruding abnormally through a tear or opening in an adjacent part)
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish فتق (fıtık), itself from Arabic فَتْق (fatq, “hernia”), in dialects فِتْق (fitq).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish غدار, from Arabic غَدَّار (ḡaddār).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish غافل (gafil), from Arabic غَافِل (ḡāfil), active participle of غَفَلَ (ḡafala).
From Ottoman Turkish غفلت, from Arabic غَفْلَة (ḡafla).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish غائب (gâʾib), from Arabic غَائِب (ḡāʔib).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish غلبه (ğalebe), from Arabic غَلَبَة (ḡalaba). Doublet of dialectal kalaba.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish غلیان (ğaleyân), from Arabic غَلَيَان (ḡalayān).
From Ottoman Turkish غالبا (galiba), adverbial accusative of Arabic غَالِب (ḡālib). By surface analysis, galip + -en.
From Ottoman Turkish غالبیت (galibiyet), from Arabic غَالِبِيَّة (ḡālibiyya).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish غالب, from Arabic غَالِب (ḡālib).
From Arabic غَمّ (ḡamm).

parole.significato: dimple (skin depression, especially at corners of the mouth)
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish غمزه (gamze, “coquetry, wink or sign with the eye; dimple”), from Arabic غَمْزَة (ḡamza).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish غنی (ganî), from Arabic غَنِيّ (ḡaniyy).

Inherited from Ottoman Turkish غرابت (ġarābet, “a being away from home, in a strange town or land, absence, exile, a word's being strange or foreign, strangeness, a being strange, curious, or outlandish, singularity”), from Arabic غَرَابَة (ḡarāba, “strangeness, oddness”), verbal noun of غَرُبَ (ḡar
Ultimately from Arabic غَيْر (ḡayr). Doublet of gayr.

Inherited from Ottoman Turkish غریب (garib, “a stranger, a man away from home, strange, curious, surprising”), from Arabic غَرِيب (ḡarīb, “strange, peculiar, foreign, unfamiliar”), from غَرُبَ (ḡaruba, “to be a stranger, to be strange, odd, obscure”)..
From Ottoman Turkish غرب (garb), from Arabic غَرْب (ḡarb).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish غصب (gasb), from Arabic غَصْب (ḡaṣb).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish غیب, from Arabic غَيْب (ḡayb).
From Ottoman Turkish غایه (gaye), from Arabic غَايَة (ḡāya). Doublet of gayet.
From Ottoman Turkish غایت (gayet, “end, limit, goal; very”), ultimately from Arabic غاية (ḡāya). Doublet of gaye.

parole.significato: Letter of the Arabic alphabet: غ
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish غَیْن (gayn), from Arabic غَيْن (ḡayn).
From Ottoman Turkish غیرت (gayret), from Arabic غَيْرَة (ḡayra).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish غیری (gayri), from the third-person singular possessive form of غیر (gayr, “another”), from Arabic غَيْر (ḡayr). Compare Azerbaijani qeyri, Turkmen gaýry, Uzbek gʻayri.

Inherited from Ottoman Turkish غیری (gayrî), from Arabic غَيْرِيّ (ḡayriyy). By surface analysis, gayr + -i (nisba suffix). Cognate with Azerbaijani qeyri, Turkmen gaýry, Uyghur غەيرىي (gheyriy), Uzbek gʻayri.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish غیر منقول (gayr-i menkul), from Arabic غَيْر مَنْقُول (ḡayr manqūl). By surface analysis, gayri- (“non-”) + menkul (“movable”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish غیر ممكن (gayr-i mümkin), from Arabic غَيْر مُمْكِن (ḡayr mumkin). By surface analysis, gayri- (“non-”) + mümkün (“possible”).

Inherited from Ottoman Turkish غیر طبیعی (gayrı tabî'î) from Arabic غَيْر طَبِيعِيّ (ḡayr ṭabīʕiyy). by surface analysis, gayri- (“non-”) + tabii (“formal”). Cognate with Azerbaijani qeyri-təbii, Uzbek gʻayritabiiy and Uyghur غەيرىي تەبىئىي (gheyriy tebi'iy). Compare Persian غیرطبیعی.
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish غضب, from Arabic غَضَب (ḡaḍab).

parole.significato: ghazal (a poetic form mostly used for love poetry in Middle Eastern, South, and Central Asian poetry)
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish غزل (gazel), from Arabic غَزَل (ḡazal).

parole.significato: Any place far away from one's homeland.
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish غربت (gurbet, “a being away from home, absence and exile, perfect whiteness”), from Arabic غُرْبَة (ḡurba, “a feeling of longing for one's native land, of being a stranger”), from غَرَبَ (ḡaraba, “to go away, to depart, to withdraw, to leave”)..
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish غروب (gurub), from Arabic غُرُوب (ḡurūb).
From Ottoman Turkish غرور (gurur), from Arabic غُرُور (ḡurūr).

parole.significato: a special abdest to purify oneself from impurity after sexual activity, ghusl
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish غسل, from Arabic غُسْل (ḡusl)
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish غدا, from Arabic غِذَاء (ḡiḏāʔ, “food”) influenced by غِدَاء (ḡidāʔ, “lunch”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish غنا (gınâ), from Arabic غِنًى (ḡinan).

parole.significato: The desire to have the good qualities or things someone else has without envy; admiration, the act of looking up to som…
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish غبطه (ġıbṭa, “a commendable longing, a desire without envy or malice”), from Arabic غِبْطَة (ḡibṭa)
From Ottoman Turkish غیاباً (gıyaben), from Arabic غِيَابًا (ḡiyāban).
From Ottoman Turkish غیابی (gıyabi), from Arabic غِيَابِيّ (ḡiyābiyy).

parole.significato: absence (state of being away or withdrawn)
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish غیاب (gıyab), from Arabic غِيَاب (ḡiyāb).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish غیبت (ġıybet), from Arabic غِيبَة (ḡība).

parole.significato: Letter of the Arabic alphabet: ح
parole.testo: From Arabic حَاء (ḥāʔ).
From Arabic حَبَّة (ḥabba).
From Ottoman Turkish خبر (haber), from Old Anatolian Turkish خَبَرۡ (ḫaber), from Arabic خَبَر (ḵabar).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish حبیب (habîb), from Arabic حَبِيب (ḥabīb).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish خبيث (habîs), from Arabic خَبِيث (ḵabīṯ, “evil”).

parole.significato: The act of visiting a sacred place during certain times of the year, generally in monotheistic religions; pilgrimage.
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish حج (hac), from Arabic حَجّ (ḥajj, “pilgrimage”), from حَجَّ (ḥajja, “to overcome”).
From Arabic حَجْم (ḥajm).
From Ottoman Turkish حجز (hacz), from Arabic حَجْز (ḥajz).

parole.significato: A Muslim who has performed the Hajj; a pilgrim; a hajji
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish حاجی (ḥācci, ḥacı, “one who has performed or is on the road to perform the rites of pilgrimage in Mecca, a pilgrim, a Christian who has performed or is performing a pilgrimage to Jerusalem, a title of respect for strangers”), from Arabic حَاجِي (ḥājī), from حَاجّ (ḥājj
From Ottoman Turkish حد (hadd), from Arabic حَدّ (ḥadd).

parole.significato: in fact, indeed, as a matter of fact, actually
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish حد ذاتنده (ḥaddi zātında), from Arabic فِي حَدِّ ذَاتِهِ (fī ḥaddi ḏātihi, “in itself, per se”).

Inherited from Ottoman Turkish خدمه (ḫademe), plural of خادم (ḫadım, “a man servant, a servant”), from Arabic خَادِمْ (ḵādim, “domestic servant, employee”), active participle of خَدَمَ (ḵadama, “to serve”).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish حدیث (hadis), from Arabic حَدِيث (ḥadīṯ).
From Ottoman Turkish حادثه, from Arabic حَادِثَة (ḥādiṯa).
Inherited from Ottoman Turkish خادم (hâdım), from Arabic خادم (ḵādim). Doublet of hadim.

parole.significato: Having little weight; light, not heavy.
parole.testo: Inherited from Ottoman Turkish خفیف (ḫafif, “light in weight or degree, foolish, undignified, immoral, quick, sharp”), from Arabic خَفِيف (ḵafīf).

From Ottoman Turkish حفریات (hafriyat), employing the plural of Arabic حَفْرِيَّة (ḥafriyya).

Inherited from Ottoman Turkish حقانیت (hakkâniyyet), from Arabic حَقَّانِيَّة (ḥaqqāniyya).
